variants.note: Own proportional_system.symmetry field states 'near-symmetrical' directly. Chambord, the paradigm exemplar, is topped by 'an asymmetrical roofscape of eleven tower types and three chimney types arranged with no symmetry whatsoever' -- 'a Renaissance plan under a Gothic sky.'

CASCADE-PROVENANCE FIX. Before this override, composition_parti wrongly resolved to 'strict-bilateral-symmetry' (forbidding this very variant) sourced from renaissance-classical -- italian-renaissance's own family, spliced in per the WP-4.2 mechanism because this node's descends_from edge to italian-renaissance (weight 0.6, inherits_kit true) is real. But italian-renaissance's family generalization ('all three members... unambiguously symmetrical') does not describe THIS node: this node's own proportional_system.symmetry is literally 'near-symmetrical,' and its own family kit (continental-baroque-neoclassical) deliberately left composition_parti OPEN specifically to avoid this exact collision -- 'three of the four members state strict-bilateral... but the fourth and earliest, french-renaissance-chateau, states near-symmetrical... forcing strict-bilateral here would silently overwrite a real, sourced difference in the earliest member.' The family's own open binding does not stop a further-removed ancestor's binding from leaking through beneath it, so it has to be corrected here, on this node's own kit, per docs/inheritance.md's cascade-bug guidance.

composition_parti.rule: The wall below is symmetrical or near-symmetrical, generated on the travee grid, but the roofscape above it is not symmetrized to match -- towers, dormers and chimneys are heraldic and are not forced into an axial figure the way a French Baroque or Neoclassical roof would be.
sources: french-renaissance-chateau.json proportional_system.symmetry, exemplars (Chambord), continental-baroque-neoclassical.kit.json composition_parti note

variants.note: diagnostic_tells: 'The roof is as tall as the wall -- if the roof is subordinate, it is a later French classical building, not a Renaissance chateau.'

roof_form.rule: The roof occupies a height comparable to the wall below -- 0.8 to 1.2 times the wall height, never less than 0.7 (hard constraint c01) -- pitched 55-70 degrees. This is THE diagnostic separating this style from its own French Baroque descendant, where the roof is subordinated.

roof_material.rule: Steep roofs of 55 to 70 degrees in slate or flat clay tile (defining_characteristics).

variants.note: defining_characteristics: 'Dormers (lucarnes) rising from the wall plane, carried up as stone frontispieces with their own pilasters and pediments, aligned exactly on the travee axes.'
Hard co-occurrence constraint c02: 'a dormer floating between two windows is a hard error.' Dormer count must equal bay count (tested).

dormer.rule: Every travee carries a dormer, aligned exactly on that travee's axis and matching the bay count exactly (hard constraint c02, tested). Each dormer is a stone frontispiece with its own pilasters and pediment, standing on the wall plane rather than set back on the roof slope (diagnostic_tells).
sources: french-renaissance-chateau.json defining_characteristics, constraints c02, diagnostic_tells, proportional_system.typical_ratios

stack_height_above_ridge.note: 1/4 to 1/2 of the roof's own height, per typical_ratios.

variants.note: diagnostic_tells: 'Chimney stacks tall enough to compete with the towers, panelled and moulded on all four faces.'

chimney.rule: Chimney stacks are treated as a designed element of the silhouette, individually panelled and moulded on all four faces, tall enough to compete visually with the corner towers (defining_characteristics, diagnostic_tells).

variants.note: description.long: 'soft white tufa that weathers to grey and picks up rain in every moulding.' The croisee window is 'in light-coloured limestone or tufa against a plainer wall' (defining_characteristics).

primary_cladding.rule: Light-coloured tufa or limestone, weathering soft grey, against which the vertical travee of windows and dormers reads as bright and thin.

variants.note: defining_characteristics: 'The croisee window: a large opening quartered by a stone mullion and transom.' Quartered into four lights of roughly 2:3 each (typical_ratios).
Anachronistic by well over a century -- the sliding sash does not exist yet in this style's floruit (1515-1600).

window_type.rule: The croisee: a large opening quartered by a stone mullion and transom into four lights of roughly 2:3 each, opening approximately 1:2 overall (w:h) -- getting very large very fast once the style stops worrying about arrows (description.long).

variants.note: No historical precedent. Housed in a subordinate outbuilding off the travee grid, never breaking the dormer-per-bay alignment rule (c02) on the principal range.

garage_strategy.rule: INVENTED, no historical precedent. Subordinate outbuilding, off the travee grid.

order.rule: Same cascade bug as the other three family members (this slot wrongly forbidden by french-vernacular, spliced in through this node's own hybridizes_with edge to french-manoir). Corrected: Italian classical ornament (pilasters, candelabra panels) arrives here as an imported VOCABULARY laid over the wall, not as a governing proportional system the way it is for italian-renaissance or beaux-arts-french -- this node's own bound proportion pack (vignola-composite) is explicitly noted 'optional' and low-precedence for exactly this reason.

variants.note: The style's own vocabulary is pilaster-based (surface ornament), not column-based; a free-standing structural column is not part of the documented type.

column.rule: Same cascade correction as `order`. Not a defining feature -- the style's classical vocabulary is carried by the pilaster, not the free column.

variants.note: Hard-adjacent proportional constraint c04: 'Applied pilaster orders must not be given a full projecting entablature that interrupts a travee. In this style the horizontal system yields to the vertical one; where it does not, the building has crossed into seventeenth-century classicism.'

entablature.rule: Same cascade bug as `order`, but the correction here is the opposite of the other three family members: rather than reinstating a full entablature, this node's own hard constraint (c04) FORBIDS one from interrupting the travee. Pilasters run past a string course or die into a moulding rather than carrying an entablature -- diagnostic_tells calls this out directly: 'the ornament does not know what it is holding up.'

variants.note: defining_characteristics: dormers carried up as stone frontispieces 'with their own pilasters and pediments.'

pediment.rule: Same cascade bug as `order`, corrected with high confidence: pediments occur on the dormer frontispieces, aligned on the travee axes (c02) -- not as a centrepiece portico pediment, which belongs to the later French classical descendants.

variants.note: defining_characteristics: 'Italian classical ornament - pilasters, candelabra pilaster panels, shell niches, medallions - applied as surface to a wall it does not proportion.' diagnostic_tells: 'Classical pilasters running past a string course or dying into a moulding rather than carrying an entablature.'

pilaster.rule: Same cascade bug as `order`, corrected with high confidence and the style's own strongest documented content: pilasters and candelabra pilaster panels are applied to the wall surface as an imported vocabulary, without ever taking on the load-bearing logic (a real entablature) their Italian source implies (see `entablature`, c04).

variants.note: Not part of the documented vocabulary (candelabra pilaster panels, shell niches, medallions), which is Renaissance surface ornament rather than a classical cornice enrichment.

modillion_dentil.rule: Same cascade correction as `order`. Not documented; the wall's own ornament (pilaster panels, niches, medallions) is a different register from a classical modillion/dentil cornice.

variants.note: Not documented in this node's own text; the roof is the dominant, visible feature (roof_form), which argues against a roofline-concealing balustrade of the kind the later Neoclassical descendant uses.

balustrade.rule: Same cascade correction as `order`. Not documented, and would contradict the style's own diagnostic principle that the roof is tall, visible and dominant rather than concealed.

ornament_vocabulary.rule: Same cascade bug as `order`, corrected with high confidence: pilasters, candelabra pilaster panels, shell niches and medallions, all Italian-derived and applied as surface ornament (defining_characteristics) -- not a structural classical system.

variants.note: The common case: courtyard-u and h-plan-manor ranges (own massing_affinities, both canonical/common) are typically one room deep around the court, consistent with the wrongly-general french-vernacular figure for the ordinary range.

The exceptional case the inherited french-vernacular rule wrongly denies exists at all ('no family member has a double-pile precedent'): Chambord's Greek-cross donjon is a genuinely double-depth, centrally-planned mass, not a one-room-deep range.

depth_and_pile.rule: Ordinary courtyard ranges are single-pile, one room deep around the cour d'honneur -- but the inherited french-vernacular claim that 'no family member has a double-pile precedent' overclaims: this node's own paradigm exemplar, Chambord, is an explicitly centralized Greek-cross donjon with real depth, not a range at all.
